## Abstract

Write a brief one-paragraph abstract that describes the contents of your write-up.

## Dataset

Write a brief data description, including: how data were obtained; sample characteristics; variables measured; and data preprocessing. This can be largely based on the source paper and should not exceed 1-2 paragraphs.

The data for this analysis come from Hewitson et al. (2021), *Blood biomarker discovery for autism spectrum disorder*: A proteomic analysis, published in PLOS ONE. The data were obtained from the publicly available dataset accompanying the study, which aimed to identify blood based biomarkers for the early detection of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The dataset includes 154 subjects, 76 with ASD and 78 typically developing (TD) controls. For each subject, the dataset contains measurements of 1.317 protein measurements, each subjects diagnostic group (ASD or TD), and their total score on the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS), which assesses autism related behaviors. Unlike the original published analysis, which excluded 192 unidentified variables, this assignment retains those variables for analysis.

The raw data were processed using the provided preprocessing.R script. As an initial preprocessing step, observations containing missing values were excluded from the dataset.

The protein measurements were log transformed using base 10 to reduce skewness and make their distibutions more suitable for statistical analysis. Next, the transformed measurements were centered and scaled so that each protein had a mean of approximately zero and a standard deviation of one, allowing protein levels to be compared on a consistent scale. To reduce the influence of extreme values, standardized measurements greater than 3 were capped at 3, while those blow -3 were capped at -3. The diagnostic group and ADOS scores were left unchanged. The processed dataset was saved as biomarker-clean.RData for further analysis.

## Summary of published analysis

Summarize the methodology of the paper in 1-3 paragraphs. You need not explain the methods in depth as we did in class; just indicate what methods were used and how they were combined. If possible, include a diagram that depicts the methodological design. (Quarto has support for [GraphViz and Mermaid flowcharts](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/diagrams.html).) Provide key results: the proteins selected for the classifier and the estimated accuracy.

The researchers used three approaches to identify proteins that could help distinguish between the ASD and TD groups including random forest analysis, t-tests, and correlation analysis. Random forest analysis ranked proteins according to their importance in predicting diagnostic group, while t-tests identified proteins with statistically significant differences in levels between the groups. The third method examined correlations between protein levels and ADOS total scores to identify proteins associated with ASD severity. The researchers ranked the proteins identified by each method and compared the top 10 results from each approach. Five proteins appeared among the top 10 for all three methods and were selected as core proteins: MAPK14, IgD, DERM, EPHB2, and suPAR. This approach combined complementary methods to identify proteins based on their predictive importance, differences between groups, and relationships with symptom severity.

Next, the researchers used logistic regression to build and evaluate classifiers based on combinations of the selected proteins. They tested whether adding other candidate proteins to the five core proteins improved the model's ability to distinguish ASD from TD. To evaluate performance, the data were randomly divided into training sets containing 80% of subjects and test sets containing the remaining 20%. This process was repeated 1,000 times to reduce the influence of any single random split. The researchers compared models using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), which measures how well a model distinguishes between the two groups.

The final nine-protein panel consisted of MAPK14, IgD, DERM, EPHB2, suPAR, ROR1, GI24, eIF-4H, and ARSB. The original paper reported a mean AUC of 0.8599, or approximately 86%, with a sensitivity of approximately 83.5% and specificity of approximately 82.2%. Although these results initially suggested that the protein panel could distinguish between the groups, the paper was retracted in 2024 because the correlation analysis incorrectly included TD participants with randomly assigned ADOS scores. Consequently, the conclusions supporting the nine protein panel are considered unreliable.

### Impact of preprocessing and outliers

Tasks 1-2

```{r}

library(tidyverse)

var_names <- read_csv(
  "../data/biomarker-raw.csv",
  skip = 0,
  n_max = 2,
  col_select = -(1:2),
  col_names = FALSE,
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  t() %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(name = V1, abbreviation = V2) %>%
  na.omit()

raw <- read_csv(
  "../data/biomarker-raw.csv",
  skip = 2,
  col_select = -2L,
  col_names = c("group", "empty", pull(var_names, abbreviation), "ados"),
  na = c("-", ""),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(group))

protein_cols <- setdiff(names(raw), c("group", "empty", "ados"))

set.seed(1)
sample_proteins <- sample(protein_cols, 4)

for (protein in sample_proteins) {
  values <- raw[[protein]]
  values <- values[is.finite(values) & values > 0]
  
  hist(
    values,
    main = paste("Raw Protein Levels:", protein),
    xlab = "Protein Level",
    ylab = "Number of Subjects",
    col = "gray80",
    border = "white",
    breaks = 20
  )
  
  hist(
    log10(values),
    main = paste("Log-Transformed Protein Levels:", protein),
    xlab = "Log10(Protein Level)",
    ylab = "Number of Subjects",
    col = "gray80",
    border = "white",
    breaks = 20
  )
}




# Question 2

biomarker_untrimmed <- raw %>%
  mutate(
    subject = row_number(),
    across(
      all_of(protein_cols),
      ~ ifelse(.x > 0, log10(.x), NA_real_)
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(protein_cols),
      ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))
    )
  ) %>%
  select(subject, group, all_of(protein_cols))

outlier_counts <- biomarker_untrimmed %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(protein_cols),
    names_to = "protein",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  group_by(subject, group) %>%
  summarise(
    total_measurements = sum(!is.na(value)),
    outlier_count = sum(abs(value) > 3, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    outlier_rate = outlier_count / total_measurements
  )

outlier_counts %>%
  arrange(desc(outlier_count)) %>%
  head(15) %>%
  print()

group_summary <- outlier_counts %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_subjects = n(),
    average_outliers_per_subject = mean(outlier_count),
    median_outliers_per_subject = median(outlier_count),
    subjects_with_outliers = sum(outlier_count > 0),
    average_outlier_rate = mean(outlier_rate),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(group_summary)

wilcox.test(outlier_count ~ group, data = outlier_counts)

ggplot(outlier_counts, aes(x = group, y = outlier_count)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "gray80", color = "gray30", outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Outlying Protein Measurements per Subject",
    x = "Group",
    y = "Number of Outlying Values per Subject"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

### Methodological variations

Task 3

#### Hard Intersection vs. Fuzzy Intersection

```{r}
#| echo: false

library(tidyverse)
library(infer)
library(randomForest)
library(tidymodels)
library(modelr)
library(yardstick)
load('../data/biomarker-clean.RData')

## MULTIPLE TESTING

# Function to compute tests
test_fn <- function(.df){
  t_test(.df, 
         formula = level ~ group,
         order = c('ASD', 'TD'),
         alternative = 'two-sided',
         var.equal = F)
}

ttests_out <- biomarker_clean %>%
  select(-ados) %>%
  pivot_longer(-group, 
               names_to = 'protein', 
               values_to = 'level') %>%
  nest(data = c(level, group)) %>% 
  mutate(ttest = map(data, test_fn)) %>%
  unnest(ttest) %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  mutate(m = n(),
         hm = log(m) + 1/(2*m) - digamma(1),
         rank = row_number(),
         p.adj = m*hm*p_value/rank)

# Select significant proteins
proteins_s1 <- ttests_out %>%
  slice_min(p.adj, n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)

## RANDOM FOREST

# Store predictors and response separately
predictors <- biomarker_clean %>%
  select(-c(group, ados))

response <- biomarker_clean %>% pull(group) %>% factor()

# Fit RF
set.seed(101422)
rf_out <- randomForest(x = predictors, 
                       y = response, 
                       ntree = 1000, 
                       importance = T)

# Compute importance scores
proteins_s2 <- rf_out$importance %>% 
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(protein = rownames(rf_out$importance)) %>%
  slice_max(MeanDecreaseGini, n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)
```

In this section, we analyze the difference in the logistic regression results between protein candidates (obtained via the multiple t-tests and RF methods) joined by hard intersection and fuzzy intersection. Hard intersection refers to strictly obtaining the proteins that exist in both lists, while fuzzy intersection refers to obtaining the proteins that have similar names in both lists.

To implement the fuzzy intersection, I used a fuzzy matching algorithm that made pairwise similarity comparisons between the two lists using the Jaro-Winkler similarity metric, and included both proteins in a result list if they had a similarity score below 0.3.

```{r}
#| echo: true

## LOGISTIC REGRESSION

# Select subset of interest
proteins_sstar <- intersect(proteins_s1, proteins_s2) # proteins_s1 = proteins selected by multiple t-tests
                                                      # proteins_s2 = proteins selected by RF

# Fuzzy intersection:
# using fuzzy matching to grab elements that are similar to each other 
library(stringdist)
proteins_fuzzy <- c()
for (i in 1:length(proteins_s1)) { # compare element-wise similarity of proteins_s1 and proteins_s2
  for (j in 1:length(proteins_s2)) {
    fuzzy_score <- stringdist(proteins_s1[i], proteins_s2[j], method = 'jw')  
    if (fuzzy_score < 0.3) {
      proteins_fuzzy <- c(proteins_fuzzy, proteins_s1[i], proteins_s2[j]) # store both similar elements
    } 
  }
}
proteins_fuzzy <- unique(proteins_fuzzy) # grab the unique proteins
print(proteins_fuzzy)
print(proteins_sstar)

```

The fuzzy matching algorithm picked up 2 extra proteins, FSTL1 and FSTL3, because they are similar to each other (they are one character apart). The other proteins in the result list were also in the list obtained by hard intersection.

```{r}
biomarker_sstar <- biomarker_clean %>%
  select(group, any_of(proteins_sstar)) %>%
  mutate(class = (group == 'ASD')) %>%
  select(-group)

biomarker_fuzzy <- biomarker_clean %>%
  select(group, any_of(proteins_fuzzy)) %>%
  mutate(class = (group == 'ASD')) %>%
  select(-group)

# Partition into training and test set
set.seed(101422)
biomarker_split <- biomarker_sstar %>%
  initial_split(prop = 0.8)

biomarker_split_fuzzy <- biomarker_fuzzy %>%
  initial_split(prop = 0.8)

# Fit logistic regression model to training set
fit <- glm(class ~ ., 
           data = training(biomarker_split), 
           family = 'binomial')

fit_fuzzy <- glm(class ~ ., 
                 data = training(biomarker_split_fuzzy), 
                 family = 'binomial')

## RESULTS

# Evaluate errors for both hard intersection + fuzzy intersection on test set
class_metrics <- metric_set(sensitivity, 
                            specificity, 
                            accuracy,
                            roc_auc)

# Hard intersection
results <- testing(biomarker_split) %>%
  add_predictions(fit, type = "response") %>%
  mutate(
    actual = factor(class, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE)),
    predicted = factor(pred > 0.5, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE))
  ) 

print("Hard Intersection Results")
results %>%
  class_metrics(
    truth = actual,
    estimate = predicted,
    pred,
    event_level = "second"
  )

# Fuzzy intersection
results_fuzzy <- testing(biomarker_split_fuzzy) %>%
  add_predictions(fit_fuzzy, type = "response") %>%
  mutate(
    actual = factor(class, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE)),
    predicted = factor(pred > 0.5, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE))
  ) 

print("Fuzzy Intersection Results")
results_fuzzy %>%
  class_metrics(
    truth = actual,
    estimate = predicted,
    pred,
    event_level = "second"
  )
```

It seems like the AUC and specificity scores are slightly higher in the fuzzy intersection case compared to the hard intersection case. However, the sensitivity is lower in the fuzzy intersection case than the hard intersection case, so a trade-off is present.

```{r}
#| label: "Result Graphs"
#| layout-ncol: 2

# ROC Curves
library(pROC)
roc_obj <- roc(results$actual, results$pred)

plot(roc_obj, 
     col = "royalblue", 
     main = "ROC Curve (Hard Intersection)", 
     print.auc = TRUE,          
     legacy.axes = TRUE)

roc_obj_fuzzy <- roc(results_fuzzy$actual, results_fuzzy$pred)

plot(roc_obj_fuzzy, 
     col = "royalblue", 
     main = "ROC Curve (Fuzzy Intersection)", 
     print.auc = TRUE,          
     legacy.axes = TRUE)


# Confusion tables 
confusion_table <- table(Predicted = results$predicted, Actual = results$actual)

ggplot(data = as.data.frame(confusion_table), aes(x = Actual, y = Predicted, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 6) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Confusion Matrix (Hard Intersection)")

confusion_table_fuzzy <- table(Predicted = results_fuzzy$predicted, Actual = results_fuzzy$actual)

ggplot(data = as.data.frame(confusion_table_fuzzy), aes(x = Actual, y = Predicted, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 6) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Confusion Matrix (Fuzzy Intersection)")
```

Looking at the confusion matrices, the increase in specificity in the fuzzy intersection case is due to an increase in true positives and a decrease in false positives. The decrease in sensitivity, on the other hand, is due to a decrease in true positives and an increase in false negatives

While there was an increase in AUC scores when using fuzzy intersection to select the common proteins among the RF model and the multiple t-tests, ultimately the magnitude of increase seems very small, making it hard to determine if there was any actual statistically significant difference. Additionally, there was a trade-off seen in the logistic regression results with the proteins gathered from fuzzy intersection vs. hard intersection: while there was an increase in specificity, there was also a decrease in sensitivity, which makes deciding which of the two sets of proteins to choose more convoluted on top of the small differences. For example, if a higher true positive detection of ASD is the goal, then maybe the proteins chosen by a hard intersection is more preferable, etc. So, all in all, it is very hard to tell whether the addition of the 2 proteins made a significant impact to the results before as the differences were small and a clear trade off exists.
